newsitem.title: USA: Dlr lower at U.S. close as rate hike hopes recede.
newsitem.headline: Dlr lower at U.S. close as rate hike hopes recede.

text.p: The dollar closed weaker on Friday after a surprisingly tame inflation report prompted doubts that the Federal Reserve will soon raise interest rates and traders took profits ahead of the weekend, experts said.

A Labor Department report showed the U.S. producer price index (PPI) fell 0.4 percent in February, the largest drop since October of 1994. Excluding food and energy, PPI slid 0.1 percent lower in February.
Meanwhile, U.S. industrial production rose 0.5 percent in February, while capacity utilization inched up 0.1 percent to 83.3 in February.

Market participants seemed to pay more attention to the inflation news rather than the Fed report on industrial production and capacity utilization that showed the manufacturing sector remains in good shape. Fading hopes for a rate increase, however, weighed on the dollar on Friday.

"This is predicated on the fact that the market has decided to concentrate on the inflation factor of today's news and has disregarded what can be extrapolated as positive strong signs coming out of the capacity utilitzation numbers and the industrial production," said Hillel Waxman, a first vice president at Bank Leumi Trust Co of New York.
"But whoever is trading dollars has pretty much said they're going with the mentality that there is no hike," Waxman added.
Fed policy makers meet on March 25 to decide whether they need to tighten credit to keep price pressures in check.
The dollar traded as high as 1.71 marks in overnight trade and 124.11 yen in New York.

The mark's sharp gains against the Japanese currency also helped the dollar to rise versus the yen, traders said. Some market participants were disappointed when the dollar failed to climb above 1.71 marks on Friday.
The dollar closed at 1.6945/55 marks, down from 1.7045/48 marks at the open. Against the yen, the dollar fell to 123.45/55 from 123.80/85.

The dollar had climbed above 124 yen early in the day on a news report quoting prominent economist Rudiger Dornbusch as saying Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin would act to curb the dollar if it climbed past 130 yen. Yet the dollar erased these gains later in the session.
"That caught people's eye, but I mean, it was very quickly dispelled by the market," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
"If Rubin has something to say, we are going to here it from Rubin," Strauss said.
Profit-taking also pressured the dollar as the week drew to a close.
Robert Ryan, manager of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of New York, noted that it is Friday and everyone is finally "squaring up" the remnants of whatever positions they have.
Elsewhere, the mark traded near 72.84/87 yen in very late trade, up from around 72.50/55 yen in early dealings.
The dollar closed at 1.4570/80 Swiss francs, down from 1.4675/85 francs at the open.
Sterling rose to $1.6008/18 from $1.5955/65.
The dollar inched up to Canadian $1.3650/55 at the close from C$1.3640/45 at the open.
The Australian dollar ended at $0.7975/80, up slightly from $0.7970/75.
